 SS: „Wir setzen auf eine offene, partizipative und praxisnahe Zusammenarbeit. Regelmäßige Formate wie virtuelle „Lunch & Learn“-Sessions sollen Lehrenden die Möglichkeit geben, Projekte vorzustellen, Erfahrungen auszutauschen und Feedback zu erhalten. Ergänzend sollen klare digitale Kanäle – beispielsweise ein Newsletter, ein Wiki oder ein Miro-Raum – den Zugang zu Materialien und Informationen erleichtern.“ 
 UM: „Darüber hinaus möchten wir agile Arbeitsgruppen zu konkreten Themen fördern, etwa zur SAP-Integration in der Lehre oder zu COIL-Modellen im Prozessmanagement. Lehrende aus unterschiedlichen Hochschultypen und Regionen sollen eingebunden werden. Wichtig ist uns auch, Kolleginnen und Kollegen durch Mentoring, Feedback und Anerkennung zu unterstützen. So soll eine Community entstehen, in der sich Lehrende gesehen, gehört und wertgeschätzt fühlen.“ 
 "Welche Ideen gibt es für eine Zusammenarbeit mit anderen Academic Boards und mit SAP?" 
 UM: „Wir sehen großes Potenzial in der internationalen Vernetzung mit anderen Academic Boards, etwa in EMEA, Ibero-America, North America, Sub-Sahara, Asia Pacific, Japan und Greater China. Denkbar sind gemeinsame Forschungsprojekte, Austauschforen und COIL-Module, in denen Studierende aus verschiedenen Ländern gemeinsam an realen Geschäftsprozessen arbeiten.“ 
 SS: „Mit SAP und den University Competence Centers möchten wir gemeinsame Lehr- und Lernmaterialien wie Case Studies und Lernpfade entwickeln, SAP Days und Challenge Days an Hochschulen organisieren und SAP-Technologien als Plattform für gemeinsame Projekte nutzen. Auch die Infrastruktur der Hochschule Esslingen und der OST, beispielsweise das Low Code Lab oder die Lernfabrik SmartFactory@OST, kann für Praxisprojekte und Weiterbildungsangebote für Lehrende eingesetzt werden.“ 
 "Wenn Ihr in zwei Jahren auf 2026-2028 zurückblickt, wann war Eure Arbeit erfolgreich?" 
 SS: „Unsere Arbeit ist erfolgreich, wenn der DACH-AB eine lebendige und zunehmend selbstorganisierte Community ist. Dafür braucht es etablierte Austauschformate, die von den Mitgliedern aktiv genutzt werden, sowie konkrete Kooperationen zwischen Hochschulen – zum Beispiel Co-Teaching- und COIL-Projekte, die über den Zeitraum 2026 bis 2028 hinaus fortgeführt werd

title: Joule Studio with JEV at the Decision Boundary for Autonomous Enterprise AI Agents
author: carlosbasto
text:
Before we start: this is an independent technical experiment, not an official SAP recommendation. I use “Joule Studio 2.0” for the generation of Joule Studio used here. The SAP documentation supplied for this implementation describes these pro-code capabilities as Early Adopter Care features; commands, interfaces, and availability may change before general availability. JEV is also a newly released technology. All invoice and vendor data in this demonstration is mocked. Releasing a block makes an invoice eligible for subsequent payment; it does not itself execute a payment. 

 1 What this implementation is trying to solve 
 Agentic AI changes the risk profile of an application as soon as the model can call tools with side effects. Reading an invoice, searching vendor history, or summarizing a mismatch are relatively low-impact operations. Clearing a payment block is different: it changes the state of a financial process and can make an invoice eligible for a later payment run. 
 That is the decision point we’ll explore in this article. We will build a supplier-invoice triage agent using Claude Code, the jl CLI, Joule Studio 2.0, and JEV from TypeSafe AI. The agent gathers evidence and decides how to handle the case. Before its release tool can execute, a Python wrapper checks the evidence again and asks JEV for a constrained decision. 
 The generative model handles the conversation, tool orchestration, and explanation. JEV evaluates the proposed action. Ordinary Python maps the result to execution, review, or denial. This makes the transition from reasoning to business action explicit in the implementation and reduces reliance on unconstrained generative output by restricting the consequential decision to predefined outcomes that are enforced in application code. 

 We will go through the concepts, the development setup, the invoice scenario, and the main pieces of code, then build the solution and inspect its behavior in Joule Studio. 

 2 The technologies behind the implementation 
 2.1 Joule Studio pro-code development and the jl CLI 
 SAP documents pro-code development as a way to build Joule Studio solutions from a local IDE and terminal, using the jl CLI and optionally an AI coding agent. The documented workflow covers intent, requirements, specification, solution generation, testing, and deployment. The resulting solution remains source code that developers can inspect and extend. 
 The CLI connects the local workspace to the Joule Studio landscape. It initializes the coding-agent integration, validates the solution structure, packages the assets, and provides deployment and diagnostic commands. Claude Code works inside that environment to read the platform guidance and implement the solution. 
 There are two separate uses of AI here. Claude Code is the development tool. The deployed invoice agent has its own runtime model configuration, business tools, and execution logic. Claude Code does not become a service inside the deployed agent. 
 For the platform workflow, see SAP’s Create an Agent with the CLI and Pro-Code Workflow . 
 2.2 JEV and TypeSafe System One models 
 TypeSafe AI is the company, JEV is its model, and System One is the model category it introduces. TypeSafe announced JEV on 15 September 2026 as its first public System One model, initially in early access. 
 The design centers on a particular consumer: software. An application supplies state and typed questions, and receives answers that it can use directly in its control flow. For this project, the relevant answer is one of four values: allow , confirm , review , or deny . 
 This is more than asking for a nicely formatted response. In its System One documentation , TypeSafe describes models built for constrained judgments and probabilities, without generating a written explanation. The output space is part of the question definition. The application knows which branches it must handle before making the request. 
 That fits the release tool well. By the time release is proposed, the application has already collected business evidence. It needs a judgment about a specific action, followed by a predictable software response. The agent’s LLM remains responsible for explaining the case to the user. 
 2.3 The three TypeSafe primitives 
 TypeSafe exposes three primitives. The introduction and the individual primitive documentation explain their contracts. 

 Primitive 
 What it asks 
 What code receives 

 Choice 
 Which predefined option applies 
 A choice, probabilities, and confidence 

 Score 
 Where the state falls on an ordered rubric 
 A score, probabilities, and confidence 

 Noul 
 Whether a proposition is true 
 A value from 0 to 1 

 Choice naturally fits routing and branching. Score supports ranking or threshold-based behavior. Noul provides a probabilistic answer to a yes/no-style question. In this agent’s running request path, the release guard and completion check both use Choice. 
 The TypeSafe name should not be read as a guarantee of a correct business decision. A constrained answer can still be wrong. The useful contract is that application code can handle the defined outcomes explicitly, while evaluations determine how well the model judges the underlying cases. 
 2.4 Calibration and structured state 
 TypeSafe calls its training approach Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions , or RLCD. Its launch article describes an architecture and training objective focused on producing decisions with useful uncertainty estimates. 
 For Choice and Score, confidence is derived from the returned probability distribution. It is not simply a verbal claim that the model is certain, and it should not be assumed to equal the probability of the selected option. Noul does not have a separate confidence field. TypeSafe’s confidence documentation explains how applications can use this information to choose between automatic action, additional verification, and human review. 
 Calibration is measured across sets of predictions; it does not guarantee an individual answer. Thresholds therefore need evaluation on the application’s own cases. Later in the walkthrough, we will see that this implementation preserves confidence but does not impose a confidence threshold on release. 
 The other useful concept is state . State can be a string, a JSON object, or an array. It carries the material being evaluated; the question separately defines the judgment requested. JEV currently accepts text and structured text data, not invoice images. See TypeSafe’s State documentation . 
 In our implementation, that state describes the proposed tool call, its arguments, evidence summaries, policy, side effects, and reversibility. JEV does not connect to SAP to discover these facts. Our application supplies them. 
 2.5 Small judgments composed in software 
 TypeSafe recommends narrowly scoped questions and composition in code. Independent questions can share one state in a batched request, but one answer does not automatically become the input to another question in that batch. 
 Here, the runtime uses one focused release question after Python has assembled the risk context. This is a practical entry point for experimenting with System One models inside an agent: a named action, a defined answer space, and explicit consequences for every answer. 
 JEV is new enough that I would treat this as an architectural direction to evaluate, rather than a settled standard. What makes it interesting is the possibility of composing specialized model judgments inside ordinary software, while retaining the flexibility of an agent around them. 

 3 Development approach from intent to a Joule Studio solution 
 3.1 Prepare the development environment 
 You need access to a Joule Studio landscape with the relevant pro-code capabilities, a local Claude Code installation, and access to TypeSafe’s API. SAP’s EAC guide specifies Node.js 24 or later for the CLI. The mock scenario does not require a live S/4HANA connection, although the deployed agent still needs its platform-provided runtime model access. 
 Use SAP’s Pro-Code Setup and Anthropic’s Claude Code quickstart for installation and access prerequisites. The EAC CLI installation command in the SAP guide used for this project is: npm install -g @SAP /joule-work-dev-cli-early-adopters@latest
jl v 
 This is an EAC installation pattern, not a promise of a permanently available public npm package. Follow the package access instructions for your landscape and check the current SAP guide before installing. 
 In Joule Studio, open your user settings, go to Develop , and copy the personal Sign-in URL under CLI Authorization . Pass it to the CLI in quotes: jl login '<your Sign-in URL>'
cd supplier-invoice-triage-agent
jl init claude 
 If the folder does not exist yet, then use: mkdir supplier-invoice-triage-agent
cd supplier-invoice-triage-agent
jl init claude 
 jl init claude installs the Joule Studio development skills and creates the MCP configuration used by Claude Code. The coding agent can then work with platform-specific guidance and development tools from this workspace. SAP’s AI Coding Agent documentation explains this integration. 

 3.2 Define the business intent and refine the implementation 
 I used an iterative pro-code workflow. After initializing the workspace, I worked with Claude Code to review and refine the invoice-triage implementation inside the Joule Studio project. The focus was on validating the business behavior, the local test tools, the JEV integration, and the deployable solution structure against the intended design. 
 The implementation starts from a concise business and technical intent: Build a Joule Studio agent that triages a blocked supplier invoice. It must retrieve invoice and matching evidence, check recent invoices from the same vendor, and either release the payment block, create an AP-clerk task, or escalate.

Use local test data for the business tools.

Before any release executes:
- reconstruct the relevant invoice and vendor-history evidence;
- evaluate the proposed release with TypeSafe JEV;
- use a Choice decision with allow, confirm, review, or deny;
- and enforce the result in Python so that only an explicit allow can reach the original release tool. 
 Rather than treating this as a one-shot code-generation exercise, I used Claude Code as a development and review partner. The implementation was inspected against the requirements, with particular attention to the files that define the runtime behavior: 
 app/agent.py 
 app/agent_executor.py 
 app/decision_gates.py 
 app/jev.py 
 app/mcp_providers/agw.py 
 mcp-mock.json 
 asset.yaml 
 solution.yaml 
 The review focuses on a few concrete questions: 
 Does the agent retrieve the invoice and recent vendor history before proposing a release? 
 Is release_payment_block actually wrapped before the agent receives the tool? 
 Does the wrapper reconstruct evidence independently of the LLM reasoning? 
 Is JEV called with the intended allow , confirm , review , and deny decision space? 
 Do missing, failed, disabled, or invalid JEV decisions hold the release instead of allowing it through? 
 Does only an explicit allow invoke the original release coroutine? 
 This is the important part of the pro-code workflow: Claude Code can help generate, inspect, and refine the implementation, but the resulting source remains normal application code that can be reviewed against explicit business and technical requirements.

title: Devtoberfest Leaderboard: A Few Observations and Ideas
author: Foxi
text:
Hi Devtoberfest team, 
 First of all, I really appreciate that we now have a live leaderboard for Devtoberfest! It's a great addition that makes the event even more engaging and adds a fun competitive element. 🙂 
 While checking the leaderboard, I noticed a few things that I thought might be worth sharing as ideas for possible future improvements. 
 1. Ranking participants with equal scores 
 To illustrate what I mean, here's a concrete example from my own position on the leaderboard: At one point, I had 29,415 points and was ranked #2, with only one participant ahead of me at 29,420 points. As more participants reached 29,420 points, I naturally moved down the leaderboard. Once six participants had 29,420 points, I would have expected my 29,415 points to put me at #7. 
 However, as additional participants reached the same 29,415 points, my position continued to move down as well, eventually to #13. 
 The exact numbers aren't important here. They simply illustrate the behavior I noticed: when participants have the same score, their relative positions don't seem to remain stable. 
 Two possible approaches to handling equal scores come to mind: 
 First come, first served: Participants who reach a particular score first retain their position ahead of participants who reach the same score later. 
 Shared ranking: Participants with identical scores share the same rank. In the example above, all six participants with 29,420 points would share rank #1, while those with 29,415 points would share rank #7. 
 Either approach could make the handling of equal scores more transparent and predictable. 
 2. Exploring the full leaderboard 
 I'd also love to be able to browse the entire leaderboard rather than just the top-ranked participants. It would be interesting to explore the lower ranks and see how other participants are doing. Perhaps pagination or a "Load more" option could make this possible. 
 3. Total number of active participants 
 Another nice addition would be a counter showing the total number of participants who have earned points. It would give us a better sense of how many developers are actively taking part in Devtoberfest. 
 Just a few observations! 
 Of course, I know that leaderboard positions don't affect the final prize distribution. This isn't about fairness or prizes. It's simply about making the leaderboard experience even more enjoyable. 
 Having a live leaderboard in the first place is already a great addition to Devtoberfest, and these are just a few observations and ideas for possible improvements. 🙂 
 What do you think? Would any of these improvements make sense for the leaderboard?
